passages.title: Definition of Prosperity
passages.text:
Economists have long defined prosperity in terms of monetary value, gauging a given nation’s prosperity solely on the basis of the total monetary value of the goods and services produced annually. However, critics point out that defining prosperity solely as a function of monetary value is questionable since it fails to recognize other kinds of values, such as quality of life or environmental health, that contribute directly to prosperity in a broader sense. For example, as the earth’s ozone layer weakens and loses its ability to protect people from ultraviolet radiation, sales of hats, sunglasses, and sunscreens are likely to skyrocket, all adding to the nation’s total expenditures. In this way, troubling reductions in environmental health and quality of life may in fact initiate economic activity that, by the economists’ measure, bolsters prosperity.

It can also happen that communities seeking to increase their prosperity as measured strictly in monetary terms may damage their quality of life and their environment. The situation of one rural community illustrates this point: residents of the community value the local timber industry as a primary source of income, and they vocally protested proposed limitations on timber harvests as a threat to their prosperity. Implicitly adopting the economists’ point of view, the residents argued that the harvest limitations would lower their wages or even cause the loss of jobs.

But critics of the economists’ view argue that this view of the situation overlooks a crucial consideration. Without the harvest limitations, they say, the land on which the community depends would be seriously damaged. Moreover, they point out that the residents themselves cite the abundance of natural beauty as one of the features that make their community a highly desirable place to live. But it is also extremely poor, and the critics point out that the residents could double their incomes by moving only 150 kilometers away. From their decision not to do so, the critics conclude that their location has substantial monetary value to them. The community will thus lose much more—even understood in monetary terms—if the proposed harvest limits are not implemented.

Economists respond by arguing that to be a useful concept, prosperity must be defined in easily quantifiable terms, and that prosperity thus should not include difficult-to-measure values such as happiness or environmental health. But this position dodges the issue—emphasizing ease of calculation causes one to disregard substantive issues that directly influence real prosperity. The economists’ stance is rather like that of a literary critic who takes total sales to be the best measure of a book’s value—true, the number of copies sold is a convenient and quantifiable measure, but it is a poor substitute for an accurate appraisal of literary merit.

summaries.standard:
**Passage Summary**

**Topic**

Defining prosperity: Monetary value vs. broader measures (like quality of life and environmental health)

**Framework**

Challenge Position

**Main Point**

The traditional economist’s definition of prosperity—measuring only monetary value—fails to account for important factors such as quality of life and environmental health, and focusing solely on what is easy to quantify can seriously misrepresent real prosperity. **The Most Valuable Sentence: Appears towards the end of the final paragraph (the literary critic analogy) and in the author’s direct critique (“emphasizing ease of calculation causes one to disregard substantive issues that directly influence real prosperity”).**

**P1: Introduction—Economists’ Definition vs. Critics**

Traditional economists say prosperity equals a nation’s total monetary output, but critics push back, saying this is too narrow and ignores important stuff like the environment and quality of life. We get an example: if buying more sunscreen because the ozone is worse counts as “prosperity,” that’s clearly missing something.

**P2: Example—The Timber Community**

Shows how focusing just on money can backfire: a rural community tied to timber sees timber restrictions as a threat to their prosperity, fearing job loss and lower earnings, because they’re using the economists’ definition.

**P3: Critics’ Rebuttal—Value Beyond Wages**

Critics say the monetary-focused view overlooks that destroying the land for timber ultimately damages something residents value deeply (scenic beauty, place, and even potential property value). The fact that people aren’t moving to richer places suggests their community’s non-monetary value is huge. Without protections, they’ll lose more—even in dollars—by ruining the land.

**P4: Economists’ Counterargument—Quantifying Prosperity**

Economists argue that prosperity has to be defined by things we can measure (money), not tricky things like happiness or environment. The author pushes back: just because something is convenient to measure doesn’t mean it’s the right thing to measure—like judging a book solely by sales instead of its literary quality.

questions.prompt: Which one of the following most accurately states the main point of the passage?

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipate
explanationBlocks.body:
Main Point = Topic + Purpose (i.e. Framework)

TOPIC -- how to define prosperity.
FRAMEWORK -- present debate
AUTHOR's TAKE -- ? ?

Sometimes authors stay out of a debate passage, and it almost looked like the author was going to in this one. We toggled back and forth between the ****Economists'**** view and the ****critics'**** view.

But the second sentence of the final paragraph is the author's voice coming through (in classic form, after a ****but / yet / however****).

In the last two sentences of the passage, the author is sympathizing with the critics and saying, "Yo, economists --- just because prosperity is easier to calculate if we define it in monetary terms doesn't mean that's a ****good**** way to define it. It's not a good way to define it."

So let's look for something like, "Defining prosperity in strictly monetary terms is rightly coming under fire from critics who think that non-monetary value should also be recognized".

choices.text: According to critics, communities that seek to increase their prosperity recognize the need to gauge the value and ensure the long-term health of their local environment.
choices.explanation:
This answer says nothing about "how to define prosperity", which was the central topic of the passage, so it's not really worth considering.

This answer makes it seem like the central topic of the passage was "communities that seek to increase their prosperity", which clearly was not the main topic.

choices.text: Economists’ definition of prosperity strictly in terms of monetary value is too narrow to truly capture our ordinary conception of this notion.
choices.explanation:
This has the right feel: "defining prosperity solely in monetary value is dumb."

In the second to last sentence of the passage, the author is saying,
*emphasizing ease of calculation (the way the economists do) causes one to disregard substantive issues that directly influence* *****real***** *prosperity.*

What does the author mean by "real" prosperity? Our ordinary conception of this notion -- thriving as a species. Having a decimated ozone layer is not prosperity. Ruining the natural beauty of an area by removing harvest limitations would not be prosperity.

choices.text: If economists were to alter and expand their definition of prosperity, it is likely that the economic and environmental health of most communities would appear worse under the new definition than under the old definition.
choices.tag: Out of Scope: if definition changed / Too Strong: most
choices.explanation:
This answer makes a prediction about what would change if the economists changed their position.

The passage never got into any speculation about what would happen if economists changed their position. The passage just presented the debate and then sided with the people who think the economists hold a crappy position.

The author definitely didn't make a prediction that got as specific as ****at least 51%**** of communities would be worse off.

choices.text: In contrast with the views of economists, some critics believe that prosperity can be neither scientifically measured nor accurately defined, and as a concept is therefore of little use for economists.
choices.explanation:
The critics aren't agitating for us to throw away the concept of prosperity. They're just saying, "can't we include some non-monetary sources of value in our assessment of prosperity?"

They don't seem hopeless that prosperity ****cannot**** be accurately defined. They're just arguing that prosperity ****is not**** being accurately defined by the economists.

choices.text: While they are generally an accurate and practical measure of current economic prosperity, figures for the total expenditures of a nation do not aid in providing an indication of that nation’s future economic prospects.
choices.tag: Wrong Emphasis / Too Strong: do not aid
choices.explanation:
The central topic of the passage was "how should we define prosperity".

The central topic, according to the grammar of this answer, is "figures for the total expenditures of a nation". That's too far off to keep reading.

Even if it were on topic, it's not supported. The author isn't arguing that GDP type figures ****do not aid**** in providing ****an**** indication of future economic prospects.

The author is only saying that GDP ****does not suffice**** as the ****only**** indication of future economic prospects.

questions.prompt: The example in the passage of the timber industry and its effect on a poor rural community suggests that the critics would most likely agree with which one of the following statements?

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipate
explanationBlocks.body:
We're essentially being asked "what would the critics probably say about the effects the timber industry has on the rural community"?

First of all ... what do these critics believe? In the second sentence, we hear them saying, "We shouldn't define prosperity solely in terms of monetary value. There are other kinds of values, such as qualify of life or environmental health."

Secondly ... what effects did the timber industry have on the rural community? Well, one effect it has is bringing income to the area; the timber industry is the area's primary source of income. But if the town doesn't limit the harvesting of trees, the land on which the community depends would be seriously damaged, which would degrade the abundance of natural beauty that the local citizens highly value.

So the critics would say, "See? If you focus solely on monetary value, then you'll be like, *okay I guess we shouldn't have any harvest limitations*. But if you take into account other forms of value, such as the abundance of natural beauty, then maybe doing the harvest limitations would actually provide the best net value of prosperity."

explanationBlocks.heading: Goal
explanationBlocks.body: Look for a safely worded answer reinforcing the point of view that even though harvest limitations would lower the area's financial prosperity, it would preserve the area's prosperity when it comes to natural beauty.

choices.text: Harvest limitations have little relationship to lower wages or fewer jobs in the community.
choices.explanation:
The critics would probably be willing to accept that harvest limitations would have an effect on wages / jobs in the community.

After all, the timber industry is the area's primary source of income, and harvest limitations would probably restrain how much revenue the timber industry can bring in (and thus it would affect how many jobs they can offer or how much money they can pay their workers).

We can't match up any line in the passage with the notion that "harvest limitations have almost nothing to do with wages or jobs in the community".

choices.text: Harvest limitations should be imposed only when the limitations have wide public support in the community.
choices.explanation:
We don't have any support for the harsh, restrictive language of "harvest limitations should ****only be imposed**** when X is true".

The critics are just saying that people can get shortsighted by only thinking about the immediate economic effects of harvest limitations. The critics are pointing out that when you factor in the fact that unlimited harvests would lead to spoiling the natural beauty that locals value so much, it might be a better net value to have the harvest limitations (for *this* community).

choices.text: The advantages to the community that would be created by harvest limitations are likely to outweigh the disadvantages.
choices.explanation:
The final sentence of the 3rd paragraph provides good support for this:

*The community* *****will thus lose much more***** *-- even understood in monetary terms -- if the proposed harvest limits are not implemented.*

The author is acknowledging that if the harvest limitations are implemented, then the area will lose some income from the timber industry. But if they're not implemented, then the community will lose much more.

Thus, the advantages of the harvest limitations outweigh the disadvantages.

choices.text: Communities protest harvest limitations primarily because they do not understand the long-term monetary impact of such regulation.
choices.explanation:
This generalizes a little too much. The critics are only commenting on *this town* and its harvest limitation issue.

This answer is saying that usually the #1 reason that communities protest harvest limitations is that they don't understand the long-term monetary impact.

The critics do seem to think that when it comes to *this area,* where we can tell that by citizens' decision to stay in this poorer area that they place a lot of monetary value on the abundance of natural beauty. So if they're opposing harvest limitations then they probably aren't understanding this long-term tradeoff of monetary impact.

But it's not clear that this sort of situation would be broadly applicable to other communities that protest harvest limitations.

choices.text: It is the arguments of economists that often cause residents of rural communities to view harvest limitations more negatively.
choices.explanation:
We have no support for the idea that "economists' arguments" are why residents of rural communities resist harvest limitations.

It seems like they resist them simply because they realize the local economy depends on the timber industry.

questions.prompt: Based on the information in the passage, the author would be most likely to agree with which one of the following statements regarding the weakening of the earth's ozone layer?

explanationBlocks.heading: Research
explanationBlocks.body:
The author's discussion of the *ozone layer*, in the first paragraph, is prefaced by "For example", so we know that in addition to whatever is said in that "ozone layer" sentence, there is some bigger idea that the author also thinks is true about the ozone layer.

Explicitly, we're told that a weaker ozone layer leaves people more vulnerable to UV exposure, causing sales of hats, sunglasses, and sunscreens to go up.

Implicitly, the author is talking about the ozone layer as an example in which "defining prosperity solely as a function of monetary value fails to recognize other values, such as quality of life on environmental health".

Connecting the example of the ozone layer to that language means the author is saying, "Even though monetary value is increasing (sales of hats / shades / sunblock are soaring), we wouldn't want to say that *prosperity* is increasing, because we know the cause of these increasing sales is a sad one, a weakening ozone layer, a debit to our environmental health."

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipate
explanationBlocks.body: The phrasing "author would most likely agree" means we're being tested on what's Implied, so the answer should sound in line with the point the author was trying to convey: even though a hole in the ozone layer would cause *financial* prosperity to go up, it wouldn't cause overall prosperity to go up, so it's potentially dumb for our measurements of prosperity to only look at financial stuff.

choices.text: Paradoxically, the weakening of the ozone layer actually contributes to environmental health and quality of life.
choices.explanation: The author was saying, "Paradoxically, the **degradation** of environmental health represented by the weakened ozone layer actually contributes to *economic* prosperity".

choices.text: The environmental effects of this problem are likely to occur more gradually than the economic effects.
choices.explanation: The first paragraph gives us now way to compare *how gradually* effects are likely to occur.

choices.text: The appearance of prosperity that results from this problem has directed attention away from solving it.
choices.explanation:
At no point is the author saying, "There needs to be more attention paid to the ozone layer! People have neglected this environmental problem, because they saw the appearance of prosperity."

The author is saying, "the damage caused to the ozone layer will result in prosperity, as defined monetarily by economists, but it won't result in prosperity, as defined by our common sense about whether it's prosperous to live in a world with a busted up ozone layer."

choices.text: This problem should be regarded primarily as threatening rather than contributing to true prosperity.
choices.explanation:
This is just capturing the Author's Intent in citing the ozone layer as an example. The author was trying to illustrate the position that "defining prosperity solely in terms of money would fail to recognize other kinds of values, such as environmental health".

The ozone layer is an example where you could have a detraction to environmental health while having an enhancement in terms of money. If we analyzed prosperity purely in financial terms, we would come to the *wrong* conclusion that the damage to the ozone layer increases prosperity.

The author's point is that it doesn't increase prosperity when people have to spend money to cope with ecological damage.

choices.text: This problem has resulted in part from the failure of economists to recognize it in its formative stages.
choices.tag: Unsupported Causal Relationship / Offends Common Sense
choices.explanation:
The author is not blaming *economists* for having failed to recognize the early stages of the ozone layer's decline.

Why would economists even be monitoring the ozone layer for early signs of decline? Isn't that more the job of an environmental scientist?

questions.prompt: According to the passage, economists defend their concept of prosperity in which one of the following ways?

choices.text: by claiming that alternative definitions of the concept would not be easily quantifiable

questions.prompt: The author compares the economists' position to that of a literary critic ( final sentence of the passage ) primarily to

choices.text: introduce the idea that the assessment of worth is basically subjective
advocate an innovative method of measuring literary merit
suggest that quality of life is mainly an aesthetic issue

questions.prompt: In the passage, the author cites which one of the following claims?

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipate
explanationBlocks.body: There's no way to limit our attention to one part of the passage, so let's head into the answers.

choices.text: that hats, sunglasses, and sunscreens provide an adequate substitute for the ozone layer
choices.explanation:
I can imagine the chairperson of a polluting company making this extreme argument that, "We don't need an ozone layer as long as we've got Ray-Ban's, Trucker Caps, and SPF 50".

But the author never suggested that accessories and sunblock could replace the entire ozone layer.

choices.text: that environmental protection measures are unpopular and often rejected by communities
choices.explanation:
This is overly general. There is a citation in the 2nd paragraph of ****one**** community protesting ****one**** environmental protection measure. It seemed unpopular. They seemed to reject it.

But the author never cited a generalization that these measures *typically* are unpopular and *often* get rejected.

choices.text: that the value of a locale’s environment can be gauged by the incomes of its residents
choices.tag: Out of Scope: gauge locale's value / Out of Scope: incomes of its residents
choices.explanation:
The author never cites any way to gauge the value of a locale's environment, nor does she ever talk about the incomes of a locale's residents.

In the 2nd paragraph, she mentions that the timber industry is a primary source of income to a certain community. That's the closest we get.

choices.text: that timber harvest limits are needed to save one area from environmental damage
choices.explanation:
The second sentence of the 3rd paragraph supports this answer.

*Without the harvest limitations, the land on which the community depends would be seriously damaged*.

Because the question asks which claim is cited by the author, people may have been nervous to pick this, thinking, "Wait, the *critics* said this, not the author. It says '****they say****' referring to the critics."

The verb *to cite* is where we get the word *citation.* These mean the same as *to attribute a claim* to someone or to make an *attribution*.

In other words, the question stem was literally asking, "Which of these answers is something the author quoted someone else saying?"

If it came directly from the author's brain, the stem would say
"the author *makes* which one of the following claims", not *cites* which claim.

choices.text: that most nations measure their own prosperity in terms broader than monetary value
choices.explanation: The passage never discusses any specific nations, nor does it ever generalize about what's true in ****over 50%**** of nations.

questions.prompt: The primary purpose of the passage is to

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipate
explanationBlocks.body:
For *Primary Purpose* questions, we lean on our Framework for a prephrase.

For this passage, we probably used *Present Debate* or *Challenge Position*, because the author is ultimately taking the side of critics and arguing against the economists.

Economists like to define prosperity in terms of monetary value, and our author wrote this passage to present and endorse objections to that point of view.

So let's look for something like, "to criticize the way economists usually define prosperity".

choices.text: argue that there is an inherent and potentially detrimental conflict between two schools of thought concerning a certain concept
choices.explanation:
This answer correctly suggests that there is a debate (between economists, who want to defined prosperity in strictly financial terms, and critics, who think that prosperity needs to be measured in non-monetary ways as well).

But the author doesn't present this debate to ultimately lament that there is a potentially detrimental conflict between these two sides. She isn't a dispassionate moderator who is just presenting the debate. She is involved in it.

She presents this debate to agree with the critics.

choices.text: summarize and illustrate the main points of the conflict between two schools of thought over the definition of a certain concept
choices.explanation:
This feels true but incomplete. The passage is discussing the main points between two schools of thought (economists vs. critics) in regards to the definition of the concept "prosperity".

But we should be turned off by the neutral sounding verbs "summarize and illustrate". The final two sentences are clearly coming from the author's voice, and she is taking the side of the critics against the economists.

When our author clearly expressed an opinion, then the purpose should sound more opinionated.

choices.text: question one school of thought’s definition of a certain concept and suggest several possible alternative definitions
choices.explanation:
The passage was definitely questioning the school of thought known as economics, in regards to how it defines the certain concept of "prosperity".

This vibes well with the *Challenge Position* feel we were looking for.

Did the author suggest several possible alternative definitions?

No. The author mentioned things that are left out of the "purely monetary" definition, but the author doesn't offer any alternative definitions.

choices.text: criticize one school of thought’s definition of a certain concept by providing examples that illustrate the implications of adhering to this definition
choices.explanation:
The passage was definitely criticizing the school of thought known as economics, in regards to how it defines the certain concept of "prosperity".

This vibes well with the *Challenge Position* feel we were looking for.

Did the author provide examples illustrating the implications of adhering to the economists' definition of prosperity in purely monetary terms?

Yes, an increase in the sales of hats / shades / sunscreen would look like an increase in prosperity in terms of their definition, but if it's resulting from the ozone layer's weakening ability to protect us from UV harm, shouldn't we consider that a *decrease* in prosperity?

An increase in money from unlimited timber harvesting would increase prosperity in terms of the economists' definition, but since unlimited harvesting would seriously damage the land the community relies on and the natural beauty they appreciate, this should be considered a *decrease* in prosperity.

choices.text: bring one school of thought’s perspective to bear on a concept traditionally considered to be the exclusive territory of another school of thought
choices.explanation:
The two "schools of thought" in this passage would be
1) economists: define prosperity purely in terms of money
2) critics/author: define prosperity in terms of money and also some non-monetary factors

The author didn't write a passage to say that one of those schools of thought is now venturing into a field dominated exclusively by the other school of thought. Naturally these two schools of thought wouldn't normally intermingle, because they are just contradictions of each other.

This answer would describe a hypothetical passage in which the perspective of math is brought to bear on a concept like beauty, which is traditionally considered to be the exclusive territory of aesthetics / art criticism.

passages.title: Joy Kogawa’s Obasan
passages.text:
Joy Kogawa’s *Obasan* is an account of a Japanese-Canadian family’s experiences during World War II. The events are seen from the viewpoint of a young girl who watches her family disintegrate as it undergoes the relocation that occurred in both Canada and the United States. Although the experience depicted in *Obasan* is mainly one of dislocation, Kogawa employs subtle techniques that serve to emphasize her major character’s heroism and to critique the majority culture. The former end is achieved through the novel’s form and the latter through the symbols it employs.

The form of the novel parallels the three-stage structure noted by anthropologists in their studies of rites of passage. According to these anthropologists, a rite of passage begins with separation from a position of security in a highly structured society; proceeds to alienation in a deathlike state where one is stripped of status, property, and rank; and concludes with reintegration into society accompanied by a heightened status gained as a result of the second stage. The process thus has the effect of transforming a society’s victim into a hero. The first eleven chapters of *Obasan* situate the young protagonist Naomi Nakane in a close-knit, securely placed family within Vancouver society. Chapters 12–32 chronicle the fall into alienation, when Naomi’s family is dislodged from its structured social niche and removed from the city into work camps or exile. Separated from her parents, Naomi follows her aunt Aya Obasan to the ghost town of Slocan, where Naomi joins the surrogate family of her uncle and aunt. In chapters 33–39 this surrogate family nurtures Naomi as she develops toward a final integration with the larger society and with herself: as an adult, when she receives a bundle of family documents and letters from her aunt, Naomi breaks through the personal and cultural screens of silence and secretiveness that have enshrouded her past, and reconciles herself with her history.

Kogawa’s use of motifs drawn from Christian rituals and symbols forms a subtle critique of the professed ethics of the majority culture that has shunned Naomi. In one example of such symbolism, Naomi’s reacquaintance with her past is compared with the biblical story of turning stone into bread. The bundle of documents—which Kogawa refers to as “stone-hard facts”—brings Naomi to the recognition of her country’s abuse of her people. But implicit in these hard facts, Kogawa suggests, is also the “bread” of a spiritual sustenance that will allow Naomi to affirm the durability of her people and herself. Through the careful deployment of structure and symbol, Kogawa thus manages to turn Naomi’s experience—and by extension the wartime experiences of many Japanese Canadians—into a journey of heroic transformation and a critique of the majority culture.

summaries.standard:
**Passage Summary**

**Topic**

Joy Kogawa’s novel *Obasan* and its techniques for depicting the Japanese-Canadian WWII experience

**Framework**

Highlight Noteworthy

**Main Point**

Through the structure and symbolism in *Obasan*, Kogawa both celebrates the heroism of her protagonist and subtly critiques the Canadian majority culture that oppressed Japanese Canadians during WWII.
**The Most Valuable Sentence:** The end of the third paragraph sums this up: "Through the careful deployment of structure and symbol, Kogawa thus manages to turn Naomi’s experience—and by extension the wartime experiences of many Japanese Canadians—into a journey of heroic transformation and a critique of the majority culture."

**P1: Overview and Purpose of *Obasan***

The passage introduces *Obasan* as a novel focused on the trauma and dislocation experienced by a Japanese-Canadian family in WWII. It then explains that Kogawa uses literary techniques to highlight both the protagonist’s heroism and critique the dominant culture.

**P2: The Structure of Hero’s Journey**

Here, the author analyzes the book’s form, comparing it to the three stages of a rite of passage: separation, alienation, and reintegration. The journey mirrors that of Naomi, the protagonist, as she endures loss, finds a surrogate family, and finally reconciles with her identity and past—emerging as a hero.

**P3: Symbolism and Cultural Critique**

The final paragraph discusses Kogawa’s use of Christian ritual imagery and symbolism (like “stone-hard facts” turning into spiritual “bread”) to highlight the hypocrisy of the majority culture while also giving Naomi’s journey a sense of resilience and affirmation. The passage wraps up by saying these literary devices transform both Naomi’s and the broader Japanese-Canadian community’s painful experiences into a story of heroism and critique.

questions.prompt: It can be inferred that the heroism Naomi gains in the course of *Obasan* is manifested in her

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipate
explanationBlocks.body:
We might rephrase this question as, "Why is Naomi considered heroic?"

The last two sentences of the 1st paragraph warn us that Naomi's heroism is emphasized via the novel's form. The 2nd paragraph is where we hear about that form.

It takes on a 3-stage structure of a rite of passage (presumably the last one is heroic? making it through all three is heroic?). Let's look at the stages and figure out if one sounds more heroic.

1. separation from secure position in life
2. alienation in a deathlike state / stripped of status, property, and rank
3. reintegration into society accompanied by ****heightened status**** gained as a result of second stage.

It says "the process thus has the effect of transforming a society's victim into a hero".

Of the three stages, that last one sounds the most like the heroic one.

explanationBlocks.heading: Goal
explanationBlocks.body: Look for something like "reintegration into society accompanied by heightened status"?

choices.text: reconciliation with her past
choices.explanation:
We were looking for "the last stage of the 3-stage process". Instead of using the generic wording of the 3rd stage (from the intro of the 2nd paragraph), this answer is using the specific wording of the 3rd stage in Naomi's story, which happens at the end of the 2nd paragraph.

1. Chapters 1-11
2. Chapters 12-32
3. Chapters 33-39 (*Naomi develops toward a final integration ... Naomi breaks through the personal and cultural screens ... and reconciles herself with her history)*

By pairing up "Heroism" with "3rd stage" and pairing up "3rd stage" with "final integration / reconciliation with her history", we can support this answer that matches "heroism" to "reconciliation with her history".

choices.text: careful deployment of structure and symbol
choices.explanation:
Joy Kogawa, the author, carefully deploys structure and symbol.

Does the character Naomi carefully deploy structure and symbol? Of course not. This question is asking about Naomi. Naomi's heroism is manifested in Naomi's ____ .

choices.text: relationship with her surrogate family
choices.explanation:
Naomi's relationship with her surrogate family is in chapters 12-32, which is the 2nd stage of the 3-stage process.

We're looking for an answer that matches up with the 3rd stage.

choices.text: renewal of her religious beliefs
choices.tag: Out of Scope: renewal of beliefs
choices.explanation: There isn't any part of Naomi's story that we're told about that involves Naomi renewing her religious beliefs.

choices.text: denunciation of the majority culture
choices.explanation:
Joy Kogawa, the author, denunciates the majority culture through her use of Christian symbolism.

Does the character Naomi denunciate the majority culture? Not that we ever hear about.

questions.prompt: According to the anthropologists cited by the author, rites of passage are best described by which one of the following sequences of stages?

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipate
explanationBlocks.body:
We can CTRL+F the term "rites" and we'll find our support window is the 2nd paragraph.

Its topic sentence tells us that there is 3-stage "sequence" to the rites of passage.

1st: separation from a position of security in a highly structured society

2nd: alienation in a deathlike state where one is stripped of status/property/rank

3rd: reintegration into society accompanied by a heightened status gained from 2nd stage.

questions.prompt: The passage suggests that Joy Kogawa believes which one of the following about the society that shuns Naomi?

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipate
explanationBlocks.body:
The clue words are "the society that shuns Naomi". We can scan for those or use Ctrl / Cmnd + F, but they appear in the first sentence of the final paragraph.

*Joy's use of Christian motifs and symbols forms a subtle critique of the professed ethics of the majority culture that has shunned Naomi.*

Okay, what is that saying? And specifically what is it saying that Joy Kogawa believes about this culture?

How or why is Kogawa critiquing the majority culture that has shunned Naomi? A little outside knowledge helps here. This book takes place during WWII, when Japanese citizens of the U.S. and Canada were relocated into internment camps, because the majority culture was too deeply suspicious of Japanese citizens (since Japan, Germany, and Italy were the three major powers that the U.S., Canada, and its allies were fighting).

It was a shameful way to treat citizens. Obviously, just because Japanese-Americans and Japanese-Canadians had some ethnic ties to Japan, that shouldn't have made the majority culture treat them all as dangerous spies / double-agents who needed to be rounded up and basically imprisoned until the war was over.

So when we hear "bring Naomi to the recognition of her country's abuse of her people", it's presumably referring to rounding up Japanese citizens and relocating them into internment camps.

What does this have to do with Christianity? Well it's not very consistent with the professed "Love thy neighbor" ethics of Christianity to institute a "fear thy neighbor and imprison them until the war ends" policy.

explanationBlocks.heading: Goal
explanationBlocks.body: Let's look for the most supportable answer we can find, but it should have something to do with Kogawa criticizing the majority culture for pretending to be loving, caring Christians while simultaneously robbing fellow citizens of their rights in order to put them into internment camps.

choices.text: It discouraged its citizens from seeking out their heritage.
choices.tag: Out of Scope: discouraged from heritage
choices.explanation: We don't have any text to support the idea that the majority culture tried to discourage Japanese Canadians from seeking out their Japanese roots.

choices.text: It endeavored to thwart its citizens’ attempts at heroic transformation.
choices.explanation:
We don't have any text to support the idea that the majority culture tried to discourage Japanese Canadians from their attempts at heroic transformation.

This is just a *Word Salad* that is grabbing "heroic transformation" from the 2nd paragraph, where we were talking about the way in which the narrative parallel the 3-part structure of rites of passage (by the end of this rite of passage, the subject has made a heroic transformation).

choices.text: It violated its own supposed religious ethics by doing so.
choices.explanation:
This nicely stays within our Support Window (the first sentence of the final paragraph). Kogawa is critiquing the *professed* ethics of the majority culture.

Putting the word 'professed' in there is sort of like saying "his *supposed* concern for my well being". If we thought he genuinely was concerned, we wouldn't use that modifier. By saying, "his supposed concern", we're implying that "supposedly, he was concerned, but we don't think he really was."

Similarly by saying the *professed* ethics of the majority culture, rather than just saying "the ethics", it's implying that this majority culture liked to *talk* a big game about being ethical, but yet they were simultaneously doing something very unethical to their Japanese-Canadian citizens.

Another example: "He *professes* to be unbiased, but of course he sided with his girlfriend" ... this is a way to indicate some hypocrisy or insincerity.

So critiquing the *professed* ethics is saying, "your actions don't match your rhetoric. You violated your own *supposed* ethics."

choices.text: It prohibited its citizens from participating in rites of passage.
choices.explanation:
We don't have any text to support the idea that the majority culture tried to prohibit people from participating in rites of passage.

This is just a *Word Salad* that is grabbing "rites of passage" from the 2nd paragraph, which is outside our *Support Window* for this question stem.

choices.text: It demanded that loyalty to the government replace loyalty to the family.
choices.tag: Out of Scope: demanded loyalty to govt.
choices.explanation:
We don't have any text to support the idea that the majority culture said, "loyalty to the government is more important than loyalty to family".

Even if we pull in our outside knowledge of internment camps, families went there together. People didn't forsake their family to go to the internment camp. And it's not like cooperating with a government that is forcing you to relocate to an internment camp can even be thought of as an act of loyalty. It's just compliance.

passages.title: Pronghorns
passages.text:
The pronghorn, an antelope-like mammal that lives on the western plains of North America, is the continent’s fastest land animal, capable of running 90 kilometers per hour and of doing so for several kilometers. Because no North American predator is nearly fast enough to chase it down, biologists have had difficulty explaining why the pronghorn developed its running prowess. One biologist, however, has recently claimed that pronghorns run as fast as they do because of adaptation to predators known from fossil records to have been extinct for 10,000 years, such as American cheetahs and long-legged hyenas, either of which, it is believed, were fast enough to run down the pronghorn.

Like all explanations that posit what is called a relict behavior—a behavior that persists though its only evolutionary impetus comes from long-extinct environmental conditions—this one is likely to meet with skepticism. Most biologists distrust explanations positing relict behaviors, in part because testing these hypotheses is so difficult due to the extinction of a principal component. They typically consider such historical explanations only when a lack of alternatives forces them to do so. But present-day observations sometimes yield evidence that supports relict behavior hypotheses.

In the case of the pronghorn, researchers have identified much supporting evidence, as several aspects of pronghorn behavior appear to have been shaped by enemies that no longer exist. For example, pronghorns—like many other grazing animals—roam in herds, which allows more eyes to watch for predators and diminishes the chances of any particular animal being attacked but can also result in overcrowding and increased competition for food. But, since pronghorns have nothing to fear from present-day carnivores and thus have nothing to gain from herding, their herding behavior appears to be another adaptation to extinct threats. Similarly, if speed and endurance were once essential to survival, researchers would expect pronghorns to choose mates based on these athletic abilities, which they do—with female pronghorns, for example, choosing the victor after male pronghorns challenge each other in sprints and chases.

Relict behaviors appear to occur in other animals as well, increasing the general plausibility of such a theory. For example, one study reports relict behavior in stickleback fish belonging to populations that have long been free of a dangerous predator, the sculpin. In the study, when presented with sculpin, these stickleback fish immediately engaged in stereotypical anti sculpin behavior, avoiding its mouth and swimming behind to bite it. Another study found that ground squirrels from populations that have been free from snakes for 70,000 to 300,000 years still clearly recognize rattlesnakes, displaying stereotypical anti rattlesnake behavior in the presence of the snake. Such fear, however, apparently does not persist interminably. Arctic ground squirrels, free of snakes for about 3 million years, appear to be unable to recognize the threat of a rattlesnake, exhibiting only disorganized caution even after being bitten repeatedly.

summaries.standard:
**Passage Summary**

**Topic**

Why pronghorns run faster than any modern North American predator — the "relict behavior" hypothesis.

**Framework**

Highlight Noteworthy / Problem-Solution. The author presents the puzzle, the relict-behavior hypothesis, the supporting evidence (including pronghorn herding), and similar relict behaviors in other animals.

**Main Point**

The pronghorn's extraordinary speed and other behaviors are best explained as adaptations to long-extinct predators — relict behaviors. The supporting evidence (pronghorn herding, mate selection, plus parallel cases in fish and ground squirrels) increases the plausibility of relict-behavior explanations.

**P1: The puzzle and the proposed solution**

Pronghorns can run 90 km/h, far faster than any modern North American predator. One biologist proposes that pronghorns adapted to predators known from the fossil record (American cheetahs, long-legged hyenas) that have been extinct for 10,000 years.

**P2: Why biologists are wary of relict behaviors**

Most biologists distrust relict-behavior explanations because they're hard to test (the principal component is extinct). They're typically considered only when alternatives fail. But present-day observations sometimes yield supporting evidence.

**P3: Evidence for the pronghorn case**

Several pronghorn behaviors look like adaptations to extinct enemies. Pronghorns herd, which gives more eyes to watch for predators and reduces the chance any one animal is attacked — but causes overcrowding and food competition. Since pronghorns have nothing to fear from present-day carnivores, herding looks like a relict adaptation. Similarly, female pronghorns choose mates by speed and endurance, which would have been useful when fast predators existed.

**P4: Parallel cases in other animals**

Stickleback fish from sculpin-free populations still display anti-sculpin behavior; ground squirrels separated from snakes for 70,000–300,000 years still recognize rattlesnakes. But not forever — Arctic ground squirrels (snake-free for 3 million years) no longer recognize the threat.
